Prefix Sharing Is a Sorting Problem

Rong He
September 12, 2026
Abstract

LLM serving reuses KV cache by exact prefix match, so when a prompt is assembled from a set of reusable pieces — retrieved passages, tool definitions, few-shot exemplars — the order chosen for those pieces determines how much computation can be shared. Every deployed system fixes that order by a single global convention. We prove this is optimal only when requests contain at most two pieces, and asymptotically wrong in general. Our main result is a structure theorem: the minimum prefix-trie cost equals min⁡∑xH⁡w⁡(x)​tx​(H)\min_{H}\sum_{x}w(x)t_{x}(H) over binary hierarchies HH on the requests, where tx​(H)t_{x}(H) is the canonical decomposition size of the set of requests needing chunk xx. Choosing chunk orders is therefore equivalent to choosing one hierarchy over requests. The identity yields an O⁡(3m)O(3^{m}) exact algorithm, identifies the two-chunk case as minimum vertex cover, and shows that on the leave-one-out family the optimum is the minimum external path length of a binary tree — the merge-sort recursion — so a global order pays Θ⁡(n2)\Theta(n^{2}) against a true cost of Θ⁡(n​log⁡n)\Theta(n\log n). Agglomerative clustering by common intersection is a tight 12\tfrac{1}{2}-approximation for the achievable saving. On BM25 retrieval traces over three BEIR corpora the resulting layout reduces prefill by 17–36% against production RAG ordering, and the margin widens with retrieval depth as the theory predicts. Serving requests in the hierarchy’s DFS order finally lets a cache holding one request’s context attain the unbounded-cache optimum exactly, so cache capacity and reorder window act as substitutes.

Code, data pipeline, and verification scripts:
https://github.com/Darrenus/prefix-sharing-is-sorting

1 Introduction

Every production LLM serving stack — vLLM [14], SGLang [21], TensorRT-LLM, and the prompt-caching APIs of the commercial providers — reuses KV cache by exact prefix match. Two requests share computation up to the first token where they disagree, and not one token further.

That rule is cheap to implement and it is the reason prefix caching works at all. It also quietly creates an optimisation problem that no system solves globally, because in a growing fraction of real traffic the prompt is not a sentence a user typed. It is a set of reusable pieces that the system itself assembled:

  • •

    retrieved passages in RAG,

  • •

    tool / function definitions in an agent,

  • •

    few-shot exemplars,

  • •

    memory or scratchpad items carried between turns,

  • •

    system-policy fragments composed per tenant.

The pieces are a set. The prompt is a sequence. Something has to choose the order, and that choice is free — the model sees the same evidence either way. Today every system makes it with a single global convention: retrieval rank, document id, popularity, insertion time. One order, applied to everybody.

The question this paper asks is whether that is the right thing to do. The answer is that it is optimal only in a degenerate regime, and asymptotically wrong in general.

1.1 Contributions

  1. 1.

    A structure theorem (Section 3). The minimum prefix-trie cost equals min⁡∑xH⁡w⁡(x)​tx​(H)\min_{H}\sum_{x}w(x)t_{x}(H) over binary hierarchies on the requests, where txt_{x} is a canonical-decomposition size. The permutations vanish: choosing orders is choosing one clustering. This gives an O⁡(3m)O(3^{m}) exact algorithm and is the engine for everything below.

  2. 2.

    The reach of global orders (Section 4). It is optimal iff every request has at most two chunks — at two chunks the problem is minimum vertex cover — and the unique minimal counterexample is the complete 3-uniform hypergraph on four chunks, 8 versus 9.

  3. 3.

    An unbounded separation (Section 5). On the leave-one-out family the optimum is the minimum external path length of a binary tree, so a global order pays Θ⁡(n2)\Theta(n^{2}) where the truth is Θ⁡(n​log⁡n)\Theta(n\log n) — the merge-sort recursion, and a Θ⁡(n/log⁡n)\Theta(n/\log n) gap.

  4. 4.

    A tight approximation (Section 6). The natural level-wise greedy hitting set attains the bad Θ⁡(n2)\Theta(n^{2}); agglomerative clustering by common intersection is a tight 12\tfrac{1}{2}-approximation for the savings, and is 0.05% from optimal on real retrieval structure.

  5. 5.

    Evaluation on real traces (Section 7). 17–36% of prefill against production RAG on three BEIR corpora, widening with retrieval depth exactly as the theory predicts; 13–23% survives a quality-preserving constraint.

  6. 6.

    Finite cache and scheduling (Section 8). The hierarchy is also a schedule: in its DFS order a one-request cache attains the unbounded-cache optimum exactly, so capacity and reorder window are substitutes.

2 Problem Formulation

Minimum Prefix Trie with Free Permutations (MPT). Given a universe UU of chunks with weights w:U→ℤ>0w:U\to\mathbb{Z}_{>0} (token counts) and requests R1,…,Rm⊆UR_{1},\dots,R_{m}\subseteq U, choose for each RiR_{i} a permutation πi\pi_{i} of its elements. Let TT be the trie of the resulting strings. Minimise

cost=∑v∈T,v≠rootw⁡(chunk⁡(v)).\mathrm{cost}\;=\;\sum_{v\in T,\,v\neq\text{root}}w(\mathrm{chunk}(v)). (1)

The cost is exactly the total prefill work, and — with a cache large enough to hold the trie — exactly the KV memory. So the same number is both the FLOP bill and the memory bill.

Two variants matter:

  • •

    OPTfree\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{free}}: each request may permute independently. Equivalently, the layout is an adaptive rule: given the prefix laid down so far, which chunk comes next?

  • •

    OPTglob\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{glob}}: all πi\pi_{i} must be induced by one linear order on UU. This is what every deployed system does.

The remainder of the paper studies the distance between these two quantities.

3 A Structure Theorem for Prefix Layout

Everything below rests on one identity. It says the permutations are not really the objects of this problem at all.

For a chunk xx, write Sx={i:x∈Ri}S_{x}=\{\,i:x\in R_{i}\,\} for the set of requests that need it. For a binary hierarchy HH on the request set [m][m] (a rooted binary tree whose leaves are the requests), write tx​(H)t_{x}(H) for the number of maximal clusters of HH contained in SxS_{x} — the canonical decomposition of SxS_{x} in the tree HH.

Theorem 1 (structure).

For every instance,

OPTfree​(I)=min⁡∑x∈UH⁡w⁡(x)​tx​(H).\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{free}}(I)\;=\;\min_{H}\ \sum_{x\in U}w(x)\,t_{x}(H). (2)

Equivalently, since a binary hierarchy on mm leaves has exactly m−1m-1 internal nodes,

OPTfree​(I)=∑iw⁡(Ri)−max⁡∑v​internalH⁡w⁡(⋂i∈leaves⁡(v)Ri).\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{free}}(I)\;=\;\sum_{i}w(R_{i})\;-\;\max_{H}\sum_{v\ \mathrm{internal}}w\Big(\bigcap_{i\in\mathrm{leaves}(v)}R_{i}\Big). (3)
Proof.

(≥\geq) Fix any layout and let TT be its trie. Map each trie node vv to the set ρ⁡(v)⊆[m]\rho(v)\subseteq[m] of requests passing through it; the family {ρ⁡(v)}\{\rho(v)\} is laminar, and we may extend it to a binary hierarchy HH. A request containing xx emits xx exactly once, so the trie nodes labelled xx have ρ\rho-sets that are disjoint and cover SxS_{x} — they partition SxS_{x} into clusters of HH. Any decomposition of SxS_{x} into clusters of a laminar family refines the maximal one, so the number of xx-labelled trie nodes is at least tx​(H)t_{x}(H). Summing with weights gives cost≥∑xw⁡(x)​tx​(H)≥minH⁡(⋅)\mathrm{cost}\geq\sum_{x}w(x)t_{x}(H)\geq\min_{H}(\cdot).

(≤\leq) Given any HH, write I⁡(B)=⋂i∈BRiI(B)=\bigcap_{i\in B}R_{i}, which is monotone decreasing in BB. Lay out top-down: at node BB, having already emitted exactly I⁡(parent⁡(B))I(\mathrm{parent}(B)), emit the chunks of I⁡(B)∖I⁡(parent⁡(B))I(B)\setminus I(\mathrm{parent}(B)) in any fixed order, then recurse into the two children. Along the root-to-leaf path of request ii the emitted sets are disjoint and union to I⁡({i})=RiI(\{i\})=R_{i}, so this is a valid layout. Chunk xx is emitted at node BB exactly when x∈I⁡(B)∖I⁡(parent⁡(B))x\in I(B)\setminus I(\mathrm{parent}(B)), i.e. exactly when BB is a maximal cluster inside SxS_{x}. So the layout has cost at most ∑xw⁡(x)​tx​(H)\sum_{x}w(x)t_{x}(H). ∎

Two remarks. Sibling subtrees are not required to begin with distinct chunks: if they collide the trie merges them and the cost only drops, so no system-of-distinct-representatives condition arises. The identity is also weight-agnostic, since the per-chunk counting never refers to depth.

3.1 Consequences

Elimination of the permutations. Choosing an order for every request is equivalent to choosing one binary hierarchy over the requests, from which the orders are read off. The operational restatement is that the design variable is a clustering of requests, not a sort order on chunks.

Relation to segment trees. tx​(H)t_{x}(H) is the canonical decomposition size of SxS_{x} in HH — the same quantity that makes a range query touch O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) segment-tree nodes. MPT is therefore: design the tree that minimises total canonical-decomposition size over a given family of sets. Every chunk is recomputed once per fragment it is split across.

Exact algorithm. M⁡(B)=w⁡(I⁡(B))+maxB=B1⊎B2⁡(M⁡(B1)+M⁡(B2))M(B)=w(I(B))+\max_{B=B_{1}\uplus B_{2}}(M(B_{1})+M(B_{2})) is an O⁡(3m)O(3^{m}) subset DP. It solves m=16m=16 in under two seconds, where brute force over ∏i|Ri|!\prod_{i}|R_{i}|! layouts died at m=7m=7. Every exact number in this paper was recomputed with it.

A tractable special case. If the family {Sx}\{S_{x}\} has the consecutive-ones property — the requests can be laid on a line so that every chunk is wanted by a contiguous run, which is what perfect topical locality would look like — then a balanced tree over that line makes each SxS_{x} an interval, and an interval’s canonical decomposition has at most 2​⌈log2⁡m⌉2\lceil\log_{2}m\rceil nodes. So OPTfree≤∑xw⁡(x)​min⁡(|Sx|,2​⌈log2⁡m⌉)\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{free}}\leq\sum_{x}w(x)\min(|S_{x}|,2\lceil\log_{2}m\rceil), and such an ordering is found in linear time by PQ-trees [1]. Two honest caveats: the bound is loose (on random C1P instances with m=16m=16 the exact optimum is 35 against a bound of 121), and it is vacuous on our retrieval traces, where the mean |Sx||S_{x}| is 2–6 while 2​⌈log2⁡m⌉≈222\lceil\log_{2}m\rceil\approx 22, so the minimum always picks |Sx||S_{x}|. It bites only for genuinely hot chunks — a shared system prompt, a tool definition, a document everyone retrieves — where it says the recomputation count is logarithmic rather than linear in the sharing.

Ordered versus free hierarchies. A global chunk order ≺\prec induces a hierarchy too: split the requests repeatedly by the ≺\prec-smallest chunk not yet emitted. So OPTglob\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{glob}} is the same minimisation restricted to hierarchies realisable by a fixed chunk priority. That is exactly the ordered-versus-free distinction of decision diagrams (OBDD versus FBDD), now stated for cache layout rather than for Boolean functions.

4 Complexity and the Reach of Global Orders

4.1 Two-Chunk Requests and Vertex Cover

Proposition 2 (two-chunk requests are vertex cover).

If every |Ri|=2|R_{i}|=2, all weights are 1, and the requests are distinct, then

OPTfree=OPTglob=τ⁡(G)+m,\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{free}}\;=\;\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{glob}}\;=\;\tau(G)+m, (4)

where GG is the graph whose edges are the requests and τ\tau is its vertex cover number.

Proof.

A layout picks, for each edge ee, the endpoint f⁡(e)f(e) that goes first. The depth-2 nodes are the mm distinct ordered pairs; the depth-1 nodes are f⁡(E)f(E), which meets every edge, so it is a vertex cover, and conversely any vertex cover induces such an ff. A global order attains it: list a minimum cover first. ∎

So MPT is NP-hard already at k=2k=2 — and at k=2k=2 adaptivity buys nothing.

Proposition 3 (the first cache level is a hitting set).

The minimum achievable depth-1 cost is the minimum-weight hitting set of {Ri}\{R_{i}\}, attained by a global order.

Proposition 3 is the honest version of the folklore rule "put the most-shared chunk first." The rule is correct — at the top level only.

4.2 The Threshold at Three Chunks

Theorem 4 (the threshold is three).

If every request has at most 2 chunks then OPTglob=OPTfree\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{glob}}=\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{free}}. At three chunks this fails, and the smallest witness is unique: U={a,b,c,d}U=\{a,b,c,d\} with the requests being all four 3-subsets. Then OPTfree=8<9=OPTglob\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{free}}=8<9=\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{glob}}.

Proof.

The layout a​b​c,a​b​d,c​d​a,c​d​babc,\,abd,\,cda,\,cdb gives the trie {a,a​b,a​b​c,a​b​d,c,c​d,c​d​a,c​d​b}\{a,ab,abc,abd,c,cd,cda,cdb\} of size 8. For the lower bound, write PdP_{d} for the partition induced by depth-dd prefixes. |P3|=4|P_{3}|=4, so cost 8 forces |P1|+|P2|=4|P_{1}|+|P_{2}|=4. A block BB at depth dd needs d≤|⋂i∈BRi|d\leq|\bigcap_{i\in B}R_{i}|; three of these triples meet in one chunk and all four in none, so blocks at depth 2 have size ≤2\leq 2 and at depth 1 size ≤3\leq 3, giving |P1|,|P2|≥2|P_{1}|,|P_{2}|\geq 2 and hence |P1|=|P2|=2|P_{1}|=|P_{2}|=2. As P2P_{2} refines P1P_{1} and both have two blocks, P1=P2P_{1}=P_{2}: the requests split into two pairs, each laying down its pairwise intersection. The three possible pairings are {a​b​c,a​b​d}/{a​c​d,b​c​d}\{abc,abd\}/\{acd,bcd\} with prefixes {a,b}/{c,d}\{a,b\}/\{c,d\} and its two images under symmetry, and each demands a,b≺c,da,b\prec c,d together with c,d≺a,bc,d\prec a,b. Contradiction; and a≺b≺c≺da\prec b\prec c\prec d attains 9. ∎

Exhaustive search over all instances on a 4-chunk universe confirms this is the only one with a gap. The minimal obstruction to a global chunk order is the complete 3-uniform hypergraph on 4 vertices.

5 An Unbounded Separation Between Adaptive and Global Orders

Let LnL_{n} be the leave-one-out family: universe [n][n], requests Ri=[n]∖{i}R_{i}=[n]\setminus\{i\}. It is the honest caricature of RAG traffic with heavy topical overlap — every two requests share all but two chunks — which is precisely the regime prefix caching is supposed to reward.

Theorem 5.
OPTglob(Ln)=(n−1)​(n+2)2=Θ(n2),OPTfree(Ln)=n⌈log2n⌉−2⌈log2⁡n⌉+n=Θ(nlogn),\begin{split}\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{glob}}(L_{n})=\frac{(n-1)(n+2)}{2}=\Theta(n^{2}),\qquad\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{free}}(L_{n})=n\lceil\log_{2}n\rceil-2^{\lceil\log_{2}n\rceil}+n=\Theta(n\log n),\end{split} (5)

so the ratio is Θ⁡(n/log⁡n)→∞\Theta(n/\log n)\to\infty.

Proof.

For the global value: LnL_{n} is SnS_{n}-symmetric so all orders cost the same, and under 1≺⋯≺n1\prec\cdots\prec n request RiR_{i} contributes n−in-i private nodes above a shared chain of n−1n-1, giving (n−1)+(n2)(n-1)+\binom{n}{2}.

For the free value, apply Theorem 1. Here Sx=[n]∖{x}S_{x}=[n]\setminus\{x\} — the complement of a single leaf. In a binary tree, the complement of a leaf decomposes into exactly the sibling subtrees hanging off its root-to-leaf path, so tx​(H)=depth​(x)t_{x}(H)=\mathrm{depth}(x). Therefore

OPTfree​(Ln)=min⁡∑xH⁡depth⁡(x)=minimum external path length of a binary tree with ​n​ leaves,\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{free}}(L_{n})\;=\;\min_{H}\sum_{x}\mathrm{depth}(x)\;=\;\text{minimum external path length of a binary tree with }n\text{ leaves}, (6)

which is the classical n⁡⌈log2⁡n⌉−2⌈log2⁡n⌉+nn\lceil\log_{2}n\rceil-2^{\lceil\log_{2}n\rceil}+n. ∎

5.1 Interpretation

Minimum external path length is why the sorting numbers appear: it is the same quantity that lower-bounds comparison sorting. The sequence 0,2,5,8,12,16,20,24,29,…0,2,5,8,12,16,20,24,29,\dots is OEIS A001855 [18], the worst-case comparison count of binary insertion and merge sort, shifted by n−1n-1, and the optimal hierarchy is the balanced binary tree — the merge-sort recursion tree.

The optimal KV-cache layout for the leave-one-out family is the merge-sort recursion tree. A single global chunk order is the bubble sort of cache layout: quadratic where the right answer is n​log⁡nn\log n.

nn adaptive (== merge sort) one global order ratio
4 8 9 1.13x
16 64 135 2.11x
64 384 2 079 5.41x
256 2 048 32 895 16.1x
4096 49 152 8 390 655 171x

6 Algorithms

6.1 Failure of Level-Wise Greedy Hitting Set

Proposition 3 suggests: at each trie node greedily take the chunk covering the most requests, split, recurse. Level-wise greedy hitting set — the algorithm anyone would write.

On LnL_{n} every chunk sits in n−1n-1 of the nn requests, so greedy peels off one request at a time and builds a caterpillar of cost Θ⁡(n2)\Theta(n^{2}): measured at n=64n=64, 2 079 — identical to the global order — against the optimum 384.

Theorem 1 says why. Greedy hitting set minimises fan-out; the objective rewards balance, because txt_{x} is a decomposition size and decomposition sizes are logarithmic in balanced trees and linear in unbalanced ones. Set-cover intuition and divide-and-conquer intuition point in opposite directions here, and divide-and-conquer wins.

6.2 Agglomerative Common-Prefix Hierarchy

Agglomerative common-prefix hierarchy. Each request starts as a singleton cluster with signature RiR_{i}. Repeatedly merge the two clusters with the largest common intersection, the merged signature being that intersection. Then walk the hierarchy top-down, emitting at each node the chunks that became common there.

This is exactly the natural greedy for the savings form of Theorem 1, which is why it works. It is O⁡(m2​log⁡m)O(m^{2}\log m) with bitset intersections and has no hyperparameters.

Quality against the true optimum. With the O⁡(3m)O(3^{m}) solver we can now measure this properly rather than argue about it. On RAG-shaped instances (mm = 10–15, kk = 5–8, Zipf pools), greedy lands 2.6% above optimal on average, 11% worst case over 72 instances. On LnL_{n} it is exactly optimal (n=16,32,64,128→64,160,384,896n=16,32,64,128\to 64,160,384,896).

That matters for reading Section 7: the double-digit margins we measure against the production baseline are genuine headroom, not heuristic slack.

6.3 Approximation Guarantee

Theorem 1 turns the algorithmic question into a clean one, and it has a clean answer.

Theorem 6.

Write SAV⁡(H)=∑v​internalw⁡(I⁡(v))\mathrm{SAV}(H)=\sum_{v\ \mathrm{internal}}w(I(v)) for the savings of a hierarchy, and let HgH_{g} be the agglomerative greedy hierarchy — repeatedly merge the pair of clusters A,BA,B maximising w⁡(I⁡(A)∩I⁡(B))w(I(A)\cap I(B)). Then for arbitrary weights,

SAV⁡(Hg)≥12​maxH⁡SAV⁡(H),\mathrm{SAV}(H_{g})\;\geq\;\tfrac{1}{2}\max_{H}\mathrm{SAV}(H), (7)

and the factor 12\tfrac{1}{2} cannot be improved.

Proof.

(i) Greedy’s merge values are non-increasing. Merging A,BA,B into CC gives I⁡(C)=I⁡(A)∩I⁡(B)I(C)=I(A)\cap I(B), so for any other cluster DD, w⁡(I⁡(C)∩I⁡(D))≤w⁡(I⁡(A)∩I⁡(D))w(I(C)\cap I(D))\leq w(I(A)\cap I(D)) — a value already available one step earlier — while untouched pairs keep their values. Hence g1≥g2≥⋯≥gm−1g_{1}\geq g_{2}\geq\cdots\geq g_{m-1}.

(ii) For every threshold θ>0\theta>0, A⁡(θ)≤2​G​(θ)A(\theta)\leq 2G(\theta), where G⁡(θ)=#⁡{t:gt≥θ}G(\theta)=\#\{t:g_{t}\geq\theta\} and A⁡(θ)=#⁡{v​ internal in ​H∗:w⁡(I⁡(v))≥θ}A(\theta)=\#\{v\text{ internal in }H^{*}:w(I(v))\geq\theta\} for an optimal H∗H^{*}.

Because w⁡(I⁡(v))w(I(v)) grows as vv descends, {v:w⁡(I⁡(v))≥θ}\{v:w(I(v))\geq\theta\} is closed under taking internal descendants; its maximal elements root disjoint subtrees T1,…,TrT_{1},\dots,T_{r} with leaf sets L1,…,LrL_{1},\dots,L_{r}, so A⁡(θ)=∑j(ℓj−1)A(\theta)=\sum_{j}(\ell_{j}-1) with ℓj=|Lj|\ell_{j}=|L_{j}|, and w⁡(I⁡(Lj))≥θw(I(L_{j}))\geq\theta for each jj.

Look at greedy at step t∗=G⁡(θ)+1t^{*}=G(\theta)+1. By (i) every currently available pair has value <θ<\theta. If two distinct current clusters A,BA,B were both contained in the same LjL_{j}, then w⁡(I⁡(A)∩I⁡(B))=w⁡(I⁡(A∪B))≥w⁡(I⁡(Lj))≥θw(I(A)\cap I(B))=w(I(A\cup B))\geq w(I(L_{j}))\geq\theta — a contradiction. So each LjL_{j} swallows at most one greedy cluster whole.

Let PP be greedy’s partition at step t∗t^{*}; the number of merges made is ∑B∈P(|B|−1)=t∗−1\sum_{B\in P}(|B|-1)=t^{*}-1. For each jj let pjp_{j} be the size of the unique block contained in LjL_{j} (zero if there is none). Any block that meets LjL_{j} without being contained in it has an element outside LjL_{j}, hence size at least 2. The LjL_{j} are disjoint, so each block contributes at most |B||B| in total across all jj, and rr is at least the number of jj having a pure block:

A⁡(θ)=∑jℓj−r≤∑B​pure(|B|−1)+∑B​impure|B|≤ 2​∑B∈P(|B|−1)= 2​(t∗−1)= 2​G​(θ).\begin{split}A(\theta)\;=\;\sum_{j}\ell_{j}-r\;\leq\;\sum_{B\ \mathrm{pure}}(|B|-1)\;+\;\sum_{B\ \mathrm{impure}}|B|\;\leq\;2\sum_{B\in P}(|B|-1)\;=\;2(t^{*}-1)\;=\;2G(\theta).\end{split} (8)

(iii) Layer-cake: SAV⁡(Hg)=∫0∞G⁡(θ)​𝑑θ≥12​∫0∞A⁡(θ)​𝑑θ=12​SAV​(H∗)\mathrm{SAV}(H_{g})=\int_{0}^{\infty}G(\theta)\,d\theta\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}A(\theta)\,d\theta=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{SAV}(H^{*}). ∎

Tightness. When every chunk is shared by exactly two requests, I⁡(v)=∅I(v)=\emptyset at any node with three or more leaves, so the savings collapse to a sum over sibling pairs and the problem is maximum weight matching — where greedy is exactly 12\tfrac{1}{2} under adversarial tie-breaking. A witness with four requests: {0123},{14},{2578},{46}\{0123\},\{14\},\{2578\},\{46\}, where greedy can take 11 against the optimal 22.

Verification. Over 3 000 random weighted instances we checked both the conclusion and the per-threshold inequality that drives it: zero violations of either. An annealed search over roughly 15 000 instances, deliberately maximising greedy’s shortfall, never got past 1.831.83 — so the worst case needs adversarial ties, and typical instances are far better (Section 6.3: 2.6% above optimal on RAG-shaped inputs).

Scope of the guarantee. This is a guarantee on savings, which is the operationally meaningful quantity — how much prefill you actually eliminated. It does not transfer to the cost: from SAV⁡(Hg)≥SAV∗/2\mathrm{SAV}(H_{g})\geq\mathrm{SAV}^{*}/2 one only gets COST⁡(Hg)≤12​(COST∗+∑iw⁡(Ri))\mathrm{COST}(H_{g})\leq\tfrac{1}{2}(\mathrm{COST}^{*}+\sum_{i}w(R_{i})), and since ∑iw⁡(Ri)/COST∗\sum_{i}w(R_{i})/\mathrm{COST}^{*} is unbounded, whether MPT itself is constant-factor approximable stays open.

A computable lower bound. Every internal node satisfies w⁡(I⁡(v))≤w⁡(Ri∩Rj)w(I(v))\leq w(R_{i}\cap R_{j}) for any i,ji,j drawn from its two subtrees, and one such cross pair per internal node forms a spanning tree on the requests. Hence SAV∗≤MaxSpanningTree⁡(w⁡(Ri∩Rj))\mathrm{SAV}^{*}\leq\mathrm{MaxSpanningTree}(w(R_{i}\cap R_{j})), so COST∗≥∑iw⁡(Ri)−MaxSpanningTree\mathrm{COST}^{*}\geq\sum_{i}w(R_{i})-\mathrm{MaxSpanningTree} — computable in polynomial time, and the only optimality yardstick available once mm outgrows the O⁡(3m)O(3^{m}) solver. It is loose (mean slack 1.45×1.45\times on random instances, and Ω⁡(m)\Omega(m) in the worst case), but it is a bound.

7 Evaluation on Real Retrieval Traces

Everything above is about a combinatorial object. This section asks whether the object shows up in real traffic, using BM25 retrieval over BEIR corpora, real passages as chunks, and real cl100k_base token counts. A request is the set of passages retrieved for one query; cost is total prefill tokens. All numbers are reproducible from code/phase2.py in the repository.

Overlap in real retrieval. On NFCorpus (3 633 passages, 2 921 queries, k=8k=8) the retrieved sets cover 2 857 distinct passages across 8 472 chunk-slots — a 2.97×2.97\times dedup factor, with 68.7% of retrieved passages wanted by more than one query and a mean |Sx||S_{x}| of 2.76. Real retrieval overlaps. The question is whether the overlap becomes prefix overlap.

Conversion of overlap into prefix reuse. Production RAG concatenates passages in relevance order, which is a per-request order, not a shared one. On NFCorpus it recovers only 6% of prefill as cache hits. A single global convention — sort every request’s passages by corpus-wide popularity — does substantially better at 13%, which is already the paper’s thesis in miniature: uncoordinated per-request freedom is worse than a convention. Coordination, not freedom, is what buys reuse.

Across three corpora and three retrieval depths (fraction of the no-sharing token bill; lower is better):

method NFC kk=5 NFC 8 NFC 16 SciFact 5 SciFact 8 SciFact 16 FiQA 5 FiQA 8 FiQA 16
relevance order (production) .844 .885 .924 .818 .867 .918 .967 .979 .990
global order by doc id .789 .831 .874 .792 .837 .900 .936 .949 .966
global order by popularity .723 .775 .832 .714 .778 .850 .842 .869 .906
online greedy longest-prefix .703 .749 .800 .695 .752 .831 .834 .861 .898
level-wise greedy hitting set .641 .661 .692 .652 .690 .732 .799 .814 .848
agglomerative (ours) .607 .605 .591 .625 .640 .643 .786 .798 .818
spanning-tree lower bound .490 .488 .465 .526 .546 .553 .660 .687 .713
savings vs production −-28.0% −-31.6% −-36.1% −-23.6% −-26.2% −-29.9% −-18.7% −-18.5% −-17.3%

Three observations follow from this table.

Production’s prefix reuse gets worse as you retrieve more. Relevance order goes .844 →\to .885 →\to .924 as kk grows from 5 to 16 on NFCorpus, and .967 →\to .990 on FiQA: at k=16k=16 over a large corpus, prefix caching has essentially stopped working. Ours goes the other way, .607 →\to .605 →\to .591. The mechanism is exactly the one Theorem 5 is about — set overlap grows with kk, but the probability that two requests agree on an entire ordered prefix collapses faster. This is the theory’s prediction showing up in a log file: the adaptive-versus-global gap widens with request size, and we measure −-28%, −-32%, −-36% at kk = 5, 8, 16.

The size of the win tracks retrieval concentration, and we report the unflattering end. NFCorpus retrieves 2 921 queries into 3 633 passages (6.7×6.7\times dedup at k=8k=8, 92% of passages wanted more than once) and gives −-32%. FiQA retrieves 2 500 queries into 57 638 passages (1.8×1.8\times dedup, 38% shared) and gives −-18.5%. So a big sparse corpus halves the benefit — and 18% of prefill is still worth having.

Distance from the optimum. Sampling real overlapping request groups (all requests retrieving a given popular passage, capped at 13) and solving them exactly with the O⁡(3m)O(3^{m}) algorithm: agglomerative greedy is 0.05% above optimum on average on NFCorpus (worst group 2.46%) and 0.00% on SciFact (worst 0.16%). Theorem 6 guarantees a factor 2 in the worst case; on real retrieval structure greedy is essentially exact, and the remaining distance to the spanning-tree bound is the bound’s looseness, not the heuristic’s.

7.1 Quality-Preserving Constraints

It might: moving a passage changes what the model attends to, and the "lost in the middle" effect says position matters. We did not run a quality evaluation, so instead we priced the constraint that removes the risk. Pin the top-tt most relevant passages, in relevance order, at the end of the prompt — nearest the question, which is where practitioners put them — and free-permute only the rest. This is also the cache-friendly shape: shared prefix, personalised suffix.

savings vs production free pin top-1 pin top-2 pin top-3
NFCorpus, k=8k=8, 2 921 queries −-31.6% −-23.4% −-17.3% −-12.9%
SciFact, k=8k=8, 1 109 queries −-26.2% −-19.4% −-13.2% −-7.9%

So the win survives the constraint: even pinning the three most relevant passages in place leaves 8–13% of prefill on the table, and pinning only the single most relevant leaves 19–23%. A quality evaluation would still be worth running, but the design does not depend on its outcome.

7.2 Online Layout with Bounded Lookahead

Requests arrive one at a time. We keep a persistent radix trie, place each arrival at its deepest usable prefix, and lay out the residuals adaptively inside each batch of WW arrivals. Savings against production (relevance order) and against the best global order:

lookahead WW 1 8 32 128 512 offline
NFCorpus vs production −-17.6% −-17.6% −-18.2% −-18.5% −-20.7% −-31.6%
NFCorpus vs best global order −-5.9% −-6.0% −-6.6% −-7.0% −-9.5% −-21.9%
SciFact vs production −-14.8% −-13.3% −-15.4% −-16.7% −-20.3% −-26.2%

The decomposition is clean. Most of the win — 15–18% against production — needs no lookahead at all: it is what you get from abandoning relevance order in favour of deepest-match placement against the live trie, which is roughly what CacheWeaver already does. The adaptive part, the thing Theorem 1 is about, adds another 5–10 points as the window grows past a few hundred and roughly doubles offline.

Comparison with a synthetic workload. An earlier version of this evaluation used a synthetic Zipf-over-topics generator and found the online curve nearly flat, concluding that adaptivity was essentially unavailable online. On real traces that is wrong: the curve rises monotonically and even W=1W=1 is far above production. The synthetic generator manufactured the difficulty by giving every topic an interchangeable pool, so there was no stable structure for a persistent trie to latch onto. We report this because it is the clearest evidence we have that synthetic workloads are not a substitute here.

What survives from the earlier reading is the interpretation of the shape: adaptivity is bought with lookahead. A global order is a convention, and conventions are what let requests that never meet still agree; below some window size you pay the coordination cost without buying the coordination. Real traffic simply has far more exploitable structure than our generator did, so the threshold sits much lower.

8 Finite Cache and Scheduling

Theorem 1 assumes the cache holds the whole trie. Real caches evict, which couples the layout with the eviction policy and the arrival order. We close that gap here, simulating the radix cache the way SGLang and vLLM actually behave: a cached node implies its ancestors are cached, and eviction removes least-recently-used leaves (code/cache.py).

Under the real arrival order, the advantage is capacity-gated. On NFCorpus (k=8k=8, 2 921 queries, one request ≈\approx 6 036 tokens), our layout’s margin over production is −-3.0% at a one-request cache, −-11.3% at 64×64\times, −-23.5% at 256×256\times, and the full −-31.7% only past 1024×1024\times. Below roughly 16×16\times every method collapses toward the no-sharing bill: at that capacity prefix caching itself has stopped working, and no layout can rescue it. The ranking, at least, never inverts — we had expected the top-heavy greedy hitting set to survive eviction better than a balanced hierarchy, and it does not.

The hierarchy also determines a schedule, which removes the capacity constraint.

Theorem 7.

Serve requests in the DFS order of the trie — equivalently, sort the stream lexicographically by the laid-out sequence. Then a radix cache with LRU leaf eviction and capacity maxi⁡w⁡(Ri)\max_{i}w(R_{i}) — one request’s context — incurs exactly the unbounded-cache cost, for any layout.

Proof.

In DFS order the requests below any trie node vv are served as one contiguous block, so vv is created at the start of its block and never needed after its end. Consider the moment request ii is served. A cached node not on ii’s root-to-leaf path either belongs to a block that has already finished — never needed again — or to one that has not started, in which case it does not exist yet. So the live set is exactly ii’s root path, of weight at most maxi⁡w⁡(Ri)\max_{i}w(R_{i}). Serving ii touches that whole path, making it strictly the most recent, so LRU evicts only dead nodes. ∎

The simulation confirms it and shows the bound is close to tight: at 0.90×0.90\times one request the cost is already exactly the unbounded-cache optimum, 0.75×0.75\times costs +0.01%+0.01\%, 0.50×0.50\times costs +0.8%+0.8\%, and only at 0.25×0.25\times does it break down (+18%+18\%). Every layout in our comparison — production’s relevance order included — hits its own unbounded-cache number at 1×1\times.

8.1 Substitution Between Capacity and Reorder Window

Reordering the whole stream is available offline; online you get a window. Sorting inside a window of WW arrivals, excess over the unbounded-cache optimum (NFCorpus, k=8k=8):

lookahead WW vs. cache 1x 4x 16x 64x 256x 1024x
1 58% 57% 54% 42% 19% 0%
128 52% 52% 52% 40% 19% 0%
512 38% 38% 38% 38% 18% 0%
2048 14% 14% 14% 14% 14% 0%
all 0% 0% 0% 0% 0% 0%

(Production in stream order at a 4×4\times cache sits at +63%+63\% for reference.)

The table is L-shaped: the excess is essentially min\min of a function of WW and a function of the capacity. Cache capacity and reorder window are substitutes — you need one of them, not both. A stack with a large prefix cache can ignore ordering entirely; a stack with a one-request cache and a deep reorder queue gets the identical number. Paying for both buys nothing.

Relation to existing schedulers. SGLang already ships cache-aware scheduling with two policies: LPM, which prioritises the waiting request with the longest prefix match, and DFS_WEIGHT, which groups waiting requests by their position in the cache tree [21]. DFS_WEIGHT is a heuristic DFS traversal. What Theorem 7 adds is the exact statement of what that heuristic is approximating and what it is worth: the target is the DFS order of the trie, and hitting it makes the required cache capacity collapse to a single request’s context — not merely better, but exactly the unbounded-cache cost, for any layout. The practical consequence is the substitution above, which we have not seen stated: a deployment does not need to buy both a large prefix cache and a deep reorder queue.

The two ideas compose. Our hierarchy supplies the layout, its DFS traversal supplies the schedule, and both come out of the same tree — so a scheduler already doing DFS_WEIGHT is running half of this paper, against a layout chosen by something else.

9 Related Work

Prefix caching in serving systems. vLLM’s PagedAttention [14] made KV cache a paged resource and automatic prefix caching a standard feature; SGLang’s RadixAttention [21] keeps prompt and generation KV in a radix tree with LRU eviction and adds cache-aware scheduling — LPM, and the DFS_WEIGHT policy discussed in Section 8.1. Both take the prompt as given. The work closest to ours in motivation is CacheWeaver [9], which states the problem exactly — "set overlap does not become reusable prefix overlap" — and resolves it with a greedy walk over a prefix tree, explicitly declining a combinatorial search. A second line attacks the same loss by weakening the exact-prefix rule instead of by ordering: Prompt Cache [11] marks up position-independent segments, CacheBlend [4] fuses KV of non-prefix chunks with selective recomputation, CacheClip [6] restores inter-chunk dependencies with an auxiliary model, and Cache-Craft [7] and PCR [20] manage per-chunk caches for RAG. None of these states a hardness result, an approximation guarantee, or an adaptive-versus-global separation, and none optimises a global objective over a request population.

Sort orders in query optimisation. The closest prior formulation we know is Guravannavar, Sudarshan, Diwan and Sobhan Babu [12], who choose sort orders for operators so that orders match across the edges of a query plan, prove a special case NP-hard, and give a 2-approximation for a join tree. The difference is precisely the content of Theorem 1: there the sharing structure — the plan tree — is given and only the orders are chosen; here the sharing structure is the decision variable and the orders fall out of it. Factorised databases [19] make the same ordered-versus-free distinction under the name of variable orders and d-trees, where a branch-dependent order can be much smaller than any global one. Trie-size minimisation under a single global attribute permutation is classical and NP-hard, including for double-array tries [13]; per-record freedom is what the RAG setting hands you and what makes MPT a different object.

Hierarchical clustering. In savings form the objective is a sum, over internal nodes of a binary hierarchy, of a monotone-decreasing set function of that node’s leaves. This puts it outside the Dasgupta family [10] and its relatives [5, 17, 8], which sum pairwise similarities weighted by a function of cluster cardinalities — indeed outside the admissibility characterisations for such objectives, which require the scaling to depend on the children’s cardinalities. We would like to know whether the sparsest-cut machinery developed there transfers; Theorem 6’s proof does not use it, and the 12\tfrac{1}{2} we get is tight for a different reason (the objective degenerates to maximum matching).

Decision diagrams. OPTglob\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{glob}} versus OPTfree\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{free}} is the ordered-versus-free distinction of branching programs [3, 25]: an OBDD fixes one variable order, an FBDD may use a different order on each path, and FBDDs can be exponentially smaller. Minimising either is hard [22]. Our Theorem 5 is an unbounded separation of the same shape in a setting where the tree is a clustering rather than a branching program; Open Problem 1 asks whether the known exponential separations transfer, which would settle the rate at Θ⁡(k)\Theta(k).

Segment trees and consecutive ones. tx​(H)t_{x}(H) is the canonical-decomposition size that makes a range query touch O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) segment-tree nodes. MPT asks for the tree minimising total decomposition size over a given family of sets; we have not found that problem studied. When the family has the consecutive-ones property a suitable leaf order is found by PQ-trees [1], giving the (loose) bound of Section 3.1.

Evaluation. Retrieval traces come from BEIR [23] — NFCorpus [2], SciFact [24] and FiQA [16] — with BM25 retrieval and cl100k_base token counts. The quality concern that motivates Section 7.1 is the position sensitivity documented by Liu et al. [15].

10 Conclusion

Prefix caching rewards requests that agree on a token prefix, but a growing share of production traffic is assembled from sets of reusable fragments whose order is chosen by the serving stack rather than by the user. This paper treats that choice as an optimisation problem and characterises it exactly. The minimum prefill cost is the minimum, over binary hierarchies on the request population, of the total canonical-decomposition size of the sets of requests needing each chunk; the per-request permutations are determined by that hierarchy and are not independent degrees of freedom. The characterisation supplies an exact algorithm, places the two-chunk case in correspondence with minimum vertex cover, and identifies the extremal behaviour as minimum external path length, so the cost of insisting on one global chunk order grows without bound.

The practical consequences follow from the same object. Agglomerative clustering by common intersection is a tight one-half approximation for the achievable saving and is within 0.05% of the exact optimum on real retrieval structure; it reduces prefill by 17–36% over the ordering production RAG systems currently use, with 13–23% surviving a constraint that pins the most relevant passages in place. The hierarchy also serves as a schedule, and traversing it depth-first reduces the cache capacity needed to reach the unbounded-cache optimum to a single request’s context, which makes cache capacity and reorder window interchangeable resources.

Two limitations bound these claims. The evaluation measures prefill tokens rather than end-to-end latency on a serving stack, so the translation to time-to-first-token depends on hardware and batch composition that we do not model. And the quality question is priced rather than measured: we report what the saving costs under a constraint that preserves relevance order, but we do not evaluate answer quality directly.

10.1 Open Problems

Theorem 1 restates each of the following as a question about hierarchies rather than about permutations, which is what makes them tractable to attack.

  1. 1.

    How much does a fixed priority cost? OPTglob\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{glob}} is the same minimisation restricted to hierarchies induced by a fixed chunk priority. We have OPTglob/OPTfree=Ω⁡(k/log⁡k)\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{glob}}/\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{free}}=\Omega(k/\log k) from LnL_{n} and a trivial O⁡(k)O(k) upper bound. Search over small universes says LnL_{n} is not extremal: the best ratios we have found by annealed search are 1.201.20 at k=3k=3 and 1.50\mathbf{1.50} at k=4k=4 ({0145,0236,1236,1245,1345,1456,2346,2356}\{0145,0236,1236,1245,1345,1456,2346,2356\} on 7 chunks: 1414 versus 2121), against L5L_{5}’s 1.1671.167 and L6L_{6}’s 1.251.25 at comparable sizes. At k=4k=4 the trivial upper bound is 44 and k/log2⁡k=2k/\log_{2}k=2, so 1.501.50 does not yet separate the two candidate rates, but it does say the leave-one-out family understates the gap by a wide margin. Is the truth Θ⁡(k)\Theta(k) or Θ⁡(k/log⁡k)\Theta(k/\log k)? This is the ordered-versus-free decision diagram question in a setting where the tree is a clustering rather than a branching program, and we do not know whether the known exponential OBDD/FBDD separations transfer.

  2. 2.

    Approximation of the cost. Theorem 6 settles the savings side: greedy is a tight 12\tfrac{1}{2}-approximation for max⁡∑vH⁡w⁡(I⁡(v))\max_{H}\sum_{v}w(I(v)). The cost side does not follow, because ∑iw⁡(Ri)/OPT\sum_{i}w(R_{i})/\mathrm{OPT} is unbounded, and we do not know whether MPT itself admits a constant factor — or whether it is APX-hard. Note the k=2k=2 case is easy to approximate (the cost is τ⁡(G)+m∈[m,2​m]\tau(G)+m\in[m,2m]), so hardness of approximation, if it holds, must come from larger requests. The related sort-order problem on a given join tree admits a 2-approximation [12], which we read as mild encouragement.

  3. 3.

    Online with lookahead. Fix a reorder window WW. What is the competitive ratio against the offline optimum as a function of WW? Section 7.2 measures a curve that rises monotonically and is still climbing at W=512W=512, and Section 8.1 shows WW trading off against cache capacity along an L-shaped frontier. We have no theory for either shape. Our guess is that Θ⁡(log⁡W)\Theta(\log W) of the log\log factor in Theorem 5 is recoverable and no more.

  4. 4.

    Beyond exact prefixes. CacheBlend [4] and CacheClip [6] trade accuracy for position-independent reuse. There the object is not a trie and Theorem 1 does not apply. Is there a formulation in which the accuracy loss and the layout cost are traded off in one optimisation?
